verses.text: Israel traveled with all that he had, and came to Beersheba, and offered sacrifices to the God of his father, Isaac.
God spoke to Israel in the visions of the night, and said, “Jacob, Jacob!” He said, “Here I am.”
He said, “I am God, the God of your father. Don’t be afraid to go down into Egypt, for there I will make of you a great nation.
I will go down with you into Egypt. I will also surely bring you up again. Joseph will close your eyes.”
Jacob rose up from Beersheba, and the sons of Israel carried Jacob, their father, their little ones, and their wives, in the wagons which Pharaoh had sent to carry him.
They took their livestock, and their goods, which they had gotten in the land of Canaan, and came into Egypt — Jacob, and all his offspring  with him,
his sons, and his sons’ sons with him, his daughters, and his sons’ daughters, and he brought all his offspring  with him into Egypt.
These are the names of the children of Israel, who came into Egypt, Jacob and his sons: Reuben, Jacob’s firstborn.
The sons of Reuben: Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi.
The sons of Simeon: Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jachin, Zohar, and Shaul the son of a Canaanite woman.
The sons of Levi: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari.
The sons of Judah: Er, Onan, Shelah, Perez, and Zerah; but Er and Onan died in the land of Canaan. The sons of Perez were Hezron and Hamul.
The sons of Issachar: Tola, Puvah, Iob, and Shimron.
The sons of Zebulun: Sered, Elon, and Jahleel.
These are the sons of Leah, whom she bore to Jacob in Paddan Aram, with his daughter Dinah. All the souls of his sons and his daughters were thirty-three.
The sons of Gad: Ziphion, Haggi, Shuni, Ezbon, Eri, Arodi, and Areli.
The sons of Asher: Imnah, Ishvah, Ishvi, Beriah, and Serah their sister. The sons of Beriah: Heber and Malchiel.
These are the sons of Zilpah, whom Laban gave to Leah, his daughter, and these she bore to Jacob, even sixteen souls.
The sons of Rachel, Jacob’s wife: Joseph and Benjamin.
To Joseph in the land of Egypt were born Manasseh and Ephraim, whom Asenath, the daughter of Potiphera, priest of On, bore to him.
The sons of Benjamin: Bela, Becher, Ashbel, Gera, Naaman, Ehi, Rosh, Muppim, Huppim, and Ard.
These are the sons of Rachel, who were born to Jacob: all the souls were fourteen.
The son of Dan: Hushim.
The sons of Naphtali: Jahzeel, Guni, Jezer, and Shillem.
These are the sons of Bilhah, whom Laban gave to Rachel, his daughter, and these she bore to Jacob: all the souls were seven.
All the souls who came with Jacob into Egypt, who were his direct offspring, besides Jacob’s sons’ wives, all the souls were sixty-six.
The sons of Joseph, who were born to him in Egypt, were two souls. All the souls of the house of Jacob, who came into Egypt, were seventy.
He sent Judah before him to Joseph, to show the way before him to Goshen, and they came into the land of Goshen.
Joseph prepared his chariot, and went up to meet Israel, his father, in Goshen. He presented himself to him, and fell on his neck, and wept on his neck a good while.
Israel said to Joseph, “Now let me die, since I have seen your face, that you are still alive.”
Joseph said to his brothers, and to his father’s house, “I will go up, and speak with Pharaoh, and will tell him, ‘My brothers, and my father’s house, who were in the land of Canaan, have come to me.
These men are shepherds, for they have been keepers of livestock, and they have brought their flocks, and their herds, and all that they have.’
It will happen, when Pharaoh summons you, and will say, ‘What is your occupation?’

that you shall say, ‘Your servants have been keepers of livestock from our youth even until now, both we, and our fathers:’ that you may dwell in the land of Goshen; for every shepherd is an abomination to the Egyptians.”

footnotes.content: Notice Jacob's first act: he stops at Beersheba and builds an altar to Isaac's God. It's not a hurried dash to Egypt. Even in upheaval, he returns to the roots of faith, offering sacrifices before he takes his household south.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God speaks in the night, calling Jacob by his name—twice, "Jacob, Jacob!"—the way we address someone we're fully present with. The Lord doesn't wait for morning or a planned moment. He meets him in the darkness with a tender, personal greeting.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The great comfort: "Don't be afraid to go down into Egypt." Jacob is old, his world is uncertain, and he's being asked to leave the land of promise. But God promises not just permission—He promises to make him a great nation there. The place changes; the promise doesn't.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I will go down with you into Egypt." What a word to carry—the Lord will not remain in Canaan while Jacob goes south alone. And then a final promise through Joseph: someone will close his eyes when his time comes. The future is already held in God's hands.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: After God's word, Jacob rises and moves. His sons carry him—their aging father, too fragile or too significant now to walk. The wagons Pharaoh sent become the means of his dignity and safety. Sometimes the Lord uses even the world's tools to keep us safe.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They pack everything: livestock, goods, the accumulation of a life in Canaan. This is not exile as punishment; it's a full household move, Jacob bringing his world with him. He's not fleeing; he's answering a call with all he owns.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Three generations travel together—sons, grandsons, daughters, granddaughters. A family held in one moment, all of them moving into an unknown land because one old man heard God say yes. The future of the covenant walks south on this road.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The chapter begins to list: "These are the names of the children of Israel." By calling them Israel—the new name God gave Jacob—the text reminds us that this household is already God's people, already chosen. The names matter because they matter to Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Reuben's sons are named—Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, Carmi—ordinary names for ordinary people, yet each one becomes part of the promise. God counts. He knows who goes down into Egypt and who will later come up again.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Simeon's line is listed; one of his sons is noted as born to a Canaanite woman. Even mixed unions, even unexpected family trees, are recorded without shame here. The covenant holds generations that don't look the way we might plan.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Levi's three sons—Gershon, Kohath, and Merari—are named here, though we may not feel their weight yet. Generations later, the Levites will carry the tabernacle. The priestly line is walking into Egypt, unaware of the calling God has for them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Judah's sons are listed, and we're reminded that Er and Onan died in Canaan. Even in a genealogy, sorrow is not erased. Yet Perez and Zerah remain—two sons born of Judah's line through Tamar, the woman who bore them outside the usual way, now part of the counted family.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Issachar's sons are named—Tola, Puvah, Iob, Shimron—simple men whose names echo through generations who will carry the calling forward. Each name is a thread in the tapestry God is weaving.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zebulun's three sons are listed. Ten sons of Israel have been named in the genealogy, but there's no sense of pride or boasting here—just a faithful record of who God is gathering into Egypt.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Leah's household is tallied: all her children and grandchildren come to thirty-three souls. And Dinah is there—the daughter, the one who suffered at Shechem, now going into Egypt with her family. She is not forgotten in the count.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gad's seven sons are named—Ziphion, Haggi, Shuni, and the rest. They go down into Egypt not knowing that their tribe will later divide the land east of Jordan, a place of their own. But God already knows.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Asher's children are listed, and Serah his sister is named—a daughter preserved in the record. She bears witness, and her name means "princess." Even the daughters of Jacob's household are held in God's memory.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zilpah's household is tallied—sixteen souls born through Leah's servant woman. There is no hierarchy in the count, no shame attached. All are numbered as part of Israel, all are going into Egypt together.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rachel's sons are named—Joseph and Benjamin—the beloved wife's children. Joseph the lost son now found; Benjamin, born after sorrow, the youngest. These two carry Rachel's own ache and hope.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joseph's two sons—Manasseh and Ephraim—born in Egypt to his Egyptian wife Asenath. They are already at home in the land where their grandfather now arrives. The family is being woven together in two worlds at once.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Benjamin's ten sons are listed—Bela, Becher, Ashbel, and seven more. The youngest son is already a father many times over, his line full and fruitful. Youth and age, sorrow and joy, are all held together in one household.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rachel's total: fourteen souls. The favorite wife's children and grandchildren—it's a smaller count than Leah's, yet her line will shape Israel's future in ways the genealogy cannot yet tell.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Dan has only one son—Hushim. Where his brother Jacob had twelve sons, Dan is here represented by his single child. Yet this one son's name is recorded, his line counted, his place secure in Israel.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Naphtali's four sons are named—Jahzeel, Guni, Jezer, Shillem. The northernmost tribe's children go into Egypt, and generations later, that northern territory will be theirs. The promise is not broken by the journey south.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Bilhah's household—the handmaid's children through Rachel—come to seven souls. They travel not as servants or outsiders but as part of Jacob's family going into Egypt. Bilhah herself is not with them now, but her descendants are numbered and safe.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The direct count: sixty-six souls descended from Jacob himself come into Egypt. The text specifies—not counting Jacob's sons' wives—these are the direct line, the seed, the promise embodied in flesh and blood.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Add Joseph's two sons, and the household becomes seventy. The number seventy carries weight—it's the number of nations in Genesis 10, the number God uses to speak of completeness. Jacob's family, now in Egypt, is a complete people.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jacob sends Judah ahead to Joseph, a path-finder to Goshen. Even in his ancient age, the father still guides his sons' steps. Judah, who once betrayed Joseph, now serves to reunite him with his father—grace works through the ones we've failed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joseph prepares his chariot and goes to meet his father in Goshen. Twenty-two years since they were torn apart. When they see each other, Joseph falls on Jacob's neck and weeps a long while—no words needed. Sometimes love speaks only in tears.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Israel's words carry the weight of a life: "Now let me die, since I have seen your face, that you are still alive." He's held the sorrow of Joseph's loss for so long that seeing him alive feels like permission to finally rest. The reunion is complete.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joseph prepares his family for Pharaoh, coaching them on what to say. This is wisdom born of living in a foreign court—he knows how to present them, how to make room for them. He's already thinking as their advocate, their interpreter between two worlds.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "These men are shepherds"—Joseph's word frames them not as refugees or outcasts but as people of a trade, a profession. They have tended flocks and herds all their lives. Work, faithfulness, skill—these are the dignity Joseph offers before Pharaoh.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "When Pharaoh summons you and says, 'What is your occupation?'" Joseph is teaching his family how to answer the powerful. There's no fear in his instruction—just preparation. He knows the question will come and wants them ready.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Say, 'Your servants have been keepers of livestock from our youth'"—the truth, simply spoken. And then the reason: so they may dwell in Goshen, apart from Egyptians who despise shepherds. Joseph has already secured them a place where they can be themselves, free from contempt. He's prepared the way.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
